os-processes-threads.title: Processes & Threads
os-processes-threads.intro: Lifecycle, fork/exec, threading models, and the cost numbers interviewers expect you to quote.
groups: Process Lifecycle & States

• States: new → ready → running → blocked → zombie → terminated. Zombie persists until parent wait()s; orphans reparented to init/subreaper.
• fork(): duplicates page tables marked copy-on-write, bumps refcounts — cheap because physical pages shared until first write faults. exec() replaces the image, keeps pid and open fds (unless FD_CLOEXEC).
• clone() flags compose everything: CLONE_VM|CLONE_FILES|CLONE_SIGHAND makes threads; CLONE_NEWNET|CLONE_NEWPID etc. make containers. pthread_create ≈ clone with sharing flags.
• exit() runs atexit handlers and flushes stdio; _exit() skips both — use after fork to avoid double-flushed buffers.
• Reaping: waitpid/WNOHANG, SIGCHLD handlers, or signalfd integration in event loops. Unwaited zombies leak PIDs.
Threads vs Processes — Real Costs

• Thread create ~10µs, process fork ~100µs+ (page-table build scales with RSS); context switch direct ~1-5µs plus indirect cache/TLB pollution up to ~100µs of lost useful work.
• Threads share heap/fds/signals-disposition; own registers, stack (default 8MB virtual on Linux), TLS, errno. Processes share nothing by default.
• vDSO: gettimeofday/getcpu resolved in user space via mapped pages — no syscall at all (~2ns vs ~100ns+ for real syscalls under mitigations).
• Fiber/goroutine: user-space scheduling M:N over kernel threads. Go GMP model: G(goroutines) queue on P(processor slots) executed by M(machine threads); blocking syscalls hand off the P so other goroutines continue.
• Interview framing: 'when threads over async?' — CPU-bound parallelism wants true threads; IO-bound massive concurrency wants M:N or event loops; mixed systems combine both.
Signals & Delivery Mechanics

• Signals interrupt execution asynchronously; handler runs on signal stack. Standard signals don't queue — multiple pending SIGUSR1 coalesce; SIGRTMIN+n realtime signals queue.
• Async-signal-safe functions ONLY inside handlers (write yes, printf/malloc no) — pattern: handler writes a byte to a pipe/eventfd, main loop reacts.
• sigaction beats signal(): explicit SA_RESTART (auto-restart slow syscalls), SA_SIGINFO (sender info), masks.
• SIGKILL/SIGSTOP uncatchable by design — graceful-shutdown choreography handles SIGTERM: stop accepting → drain with timeout → flush → exit (Kubernetes TERM then KILL after grace period).
• SIGPIPE kills naive network writers — SIG_IGN it and handle send() EPIPE explicitly.
IPC Menu & When Each Wins

• Pipes/FIFOs: simple byte streams, related procs / named. Unix sockets: bidirectional, packet boundaries option, fd passing via SCM_RIGHTS — nginx workers inherit listening sockets this way.
• Shared memory (shm_open/mmap MAP_SHARED): zero-copy fastest — sub-µs ping-pong; needs your own synchronization (futexes on shared atomics).
• message queues (POSIX/System V): prioritized messages, kernel-persistent. eventfd: efficient wakeup token for event loops. D-Bus/busd for desktop/service buses.
• File-based: locks via flock/fcntl ranges; atomic publish via rename+fsync(dir).
• Selection logic: throughput → shm; simplicity → sockets; wakeups → eventfd; compatibility → plain files.
Namespaces, cgroups & Containers

• Namespaces isolate views: pid, net, mnt, user, ipc, uts, cgroup, time. Docker = namespaces + cgroups + union filesystem images.
• cgroups v2 unified hierarchy: cpu.weight shares, memory.max triggers reclaim then OOM-kill inside the cgroup, io.max throttles IOPS/bandwidth.
• Containers vs VMs: shared kernel means near-zero startup cost and tiny images, but kernel bugs/escapes are shared-risk; VMs isolate kernels, pay hypervisor overhead.
• Rootless containers map user namespaces for unprivileged isolation; seccomp profiles trim syscall surface.
• Interview probe: 'how does docker exec work?' — same namespaces joined via setns(), new process attached to container's pid/net/mnt spaces.
Classic Interview Questions

• 'fork of a 10GB process — what happens?' Page tables duplicated (~tens of MB), COW marks entries RO, TLB flush; milliseconds not seconds; THP amplifies copy granularity (Redis disables THP for exactly this).
• 'Zombie processes — cause and cure?' Parent not reaping; cure wait()/SIGCHLD handling; orphan adoption goes to init/subreaper.
• 'How do you pass a file descriptor between processes?' SCM_RIGHTS ancillary data over unix socket — receiver gets duplicate referring to same open file description (shared offset!).
• 'What survives exec()?' PID, open fds (unless CLOEXEC), signal dispositions ignored/defaulted reset, cwd, umask, environment.
• 'Max threads/processes?' Limits: RLIMIT_NPROC, pid_max (/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max ~4M default), memory for stacks/kernel structs — practical ceiling usually memory or cgroup pids.max.

os-scheduling.title: CPU Scheduling
os-scheduling.intro: CFS, EEVDF, real-time classes, and the latency numbers behind 'why is my tail slow'.
groups: Scheduling Goals & Metrics

• Tension triangle: throughput (long batches), latency (interactive responsiveness), fairness (proportional share). No scheduler maximizes all three simultaneously.
• Metrics: turnaround time, response time, tail latency (p99), context-switch rate, fairness error (Jain's index).
• Workload assumptions matter: bursty interactive vs long compute jobs vs deadline-sensitive audio paths need different policies — hence multiple classes in Linux.
• Convoy effect: one long CPU job ahead of many short ones inflates everyone's wait — SJF fixes it but requires knowing durations; MLFQ approximates from history.
CFS — Completely Fair Scheduler

• Core idea: track vruntime = runtime × (weight₀ / weight); always run leftmost node of rbtree ordered by vruntime. O(log n) insert/pick.
• Nice levels → weights ≈ 1024/1.25^nice: nice-5 task gets roughly ⅓ CPU of nice-0 when contending.
• sched_latency target period split proportionally into slices; min_granularity prevents excessive switching under high runnable counts.
• Sleepers: vruntime clamped to min_vruntime on wake (credit for sleep, no unfairness explosion); new tasks start slightly right of min_vruntime.
• Per-CPU runqueues + periodic load balancing migrate tasks based on load tracking (PELT signals decayed averages).
EEVDF — The Modern Default (6.6+)

• Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First: tasks have lag (service deficit vs fair share) and requested slices; eligible = lag ≥ 0; pick earliest virtual deadline among eligible.
• Short slice requests → earlier deadlines → better latency without nice-value abuse; fairness provable rather than emergent.
• Replaces heuristics like sleeper bonus with principled lag accounting — fewer latency outliers under mixed workloads.
• Practical impact measured by distros: comparable throughput, tighter interactive latency distribution.
• Talking point: shows Linux still evolves fundamentals — name-drop EEVDF to signal current knowledge.
Real-Time & Priority Classes

• Linux SCHED_FIFO (run till yield/block) and SCHED_RR (round-robin within priority) preempt ALL CFS tasks; 1-99 priorities.
• SCHED_DEADLINE: EDF + CBS reservation — specify runtime/deadline/period; admission control rejects overload — audio/professional RT path.
• Danger: RT task spinning → softlockup watchdog fires; rt_throttled limits default 950ms/s per cpu group prevent lockup.
• Priority inversion: low holds lock, medium preempts it, high blocks — Mars Pathfinder reboot loop famous case; fix = priority inheritance (rt_mutex) or careful lock-free design.
• nice/ionice affect CFS/IO weights only — hard guarantees need RT classes or cgroup reservations.
Multi-Core, Affinity & NUMA Scheduling

• Wakeup balancing: try to wake task on idle sibling core (SMT awareness), else search domain hierarchy (SMT → MC → NUMA levels).
• Taskset/sched_setaffinity pinning helps cache locality and IRQ pairing but fights the balancer — pin judiciously (DPDK-style dedicated cores extreme case).
• NUMA: local vs remote memory access gap (~1.4-2x); scheduler prefers node-local placement; auto-NUMA balancing migrates pages toward accessing tasks via PROT-NUMA hint faults.
• Energy-aware scheduling (EAS) on big.LITTLE mobile: capacity-aware placement trades peak speed for power.
• Idle states: C-states trade wake latency for power; deep sleeps add µs-ms resume costs visible as tail spikes on quiet servers.
Interview Classics

• 'Design a scheduler' walkthrough: queues/classes, time slice math, preemption points, load balancing, then discuss tradeoffs vs CFS/EEVDF.
• 'Why is my p99 spiky on an idle box?' C-state exits, frequency scaling ramps, timer coalescing, background kernel threads, THP compaction — enumerate suspects with tools (perf sched, cyclictest).
• 'nice value actually guarantees?' Only relative weighting under contention — zero guarantee when uncontended or against other classes.
• 'Context switch vs mode switch?' Mode switch (syscall) stays in-process; context switch changes task (registers+address space possibly); both cost, second much more.
• Numbers to recite: switch 1-5µs, wakeup-to-run typically 5-50µs loaded, sched_period default scaled ~6-24ms.

os-synchronization.title: Synchronization Primitives
os-synchronization.intro: Mutex internals, atomics, memory ordering, RCU — the machinery underneath pthreads and every lock-free claim.
groups: Hardware Atomics Foundation

• CAS (compare-and-swap) is the universal brick: x86 LOCK CMPXCHG, ARM LL/SC pairs (load-exclusive/store-exclusive retry loops).
• Contended cacheline ping-pongs across cores via MESI coherence — the REAL cost of naive locking; false sharing (unrelated fields sharing a line) same disease: pad hot structures to 64B (alignas(64)).
• Fetch-add, test-and-set, exchange — each maps to instructions; Java AtomicInteger/Unsafe → intrinsics; Rust AtomicUsize orders parameterized.
• LL/SC note: ABA partially handled by hardware reservation granule, software must still version pointers for correctness in CAS loops.
• Memory barriers implied by atomics: relaxed/acquire/release/acq_rel/seq_cst ladder — choose weakest correct; seq_cst default safe-but-slower.
futex & Mutex Internals

• Fast path: userspace CAS on 32-bit word — uncontended lock/unlock ≈ 20ns total, NO syscall.
• Contended path: futex(FUTEX_WAIT) sleeps in kernel waitqueue keyed by address; unlocker futex(WAKE) revives one. glibc adds adaptive spinning before sleeping.
• Futex value protocol (0 unlocked, 1 locked-no-waiters, 2 locked-waiters) explains why unlock must CAS 2→0 and wake — walk through it if asked.
• Error handling subtleties: futex returns EAGAIN on value mismatch (state changed), EINTR on signals — glibc loops internally so app code stays clean.
• Robust mutexes (FUTEX_OWNER_DIED) let kernel mark locks held by crashed threads — recovery without watchdogs.
Spinlocks vs Mutexes vs RWLocks

• Spinlock: burn CPU but avoid sleep/wake latency — right when hold time < 2 context switches and preemptible contexts absent (kernel, tight critical sections).
• Mutex: park on contention — right for anything touching IO/memory-heavy sections; hybrid adaptive mutexes spin briefly first.
• RW locks: concurrent readers help read-mostly data; writer starvation risk → phase-fair RW locks alternate grants; often sharded mutex or RCU beats RW in practice (cache-line contention on reader counter!).
• Seqlock: writer bumps sequence odd→even around update; readers retry while sequence changed/odd — perfect for small read-hot values (jiffies, stats counters).
• Ticket locks give FIFO fairness under contention; MCS/qspinlock scale by per-CPU waiting nodes (Linux qspinlock evolution story).
Lock-Free Structures & Progress Guarantees

• Progress ladder: blocking < obstruction-free < lock-free (some thread progresses) < wait-free (all progress bounded).
• Treiber stack: push = CAS head; pop = CAS head->next with ABA guard (tagged pointer or epoch). Michael-Scott queue: two CAS points, dummy node simplifies.
• Hazard pointers / epochs (crossbeam, folly hazard): defer reclamation until readers done — THE missing piece that makes lock-free usable in GC-less languages.
• Practical advice: reach for proven libraries (folly, crossbeam, java.util.concurrent) — hand-rolled lock-free code is a review nightmare; say this out loud, evaluators agree.
• Know one walkthrough cold: MPSC ring buffer (LMAX Disruptor style) — sequence counters, cached consumer index, batching effects.
Memory Model Deep Cut

• Happens-before defined by program order within thread + synchronization edges between threads (release store observed by acquire load).
• Data race = conflicting accesses without happens-before, ≥1 write → UB in C++/Rust/Java — even 'benign' races are not benign under optimizing compilers.
• DCLP singleton: instance field must be atomic-acquire on read, release on store (Java: volatile; C++: std::atomic + memory_order; better: static local init magic or holder idiom).
• x86-TSO gives cheap acquire/release (loads/stores mostly ordered, store buffer only reorder) — ARM/RISC-V weaker, bugs appear porting east — why CI on aarch64 matters now.
• Java specifics: final-field freeze guarantees safe publication; VarHandle modes map to C++ orderings.
RCU & Kernel-Scale Reads

• Read-copy-update: readers run WITHOUT locking, writers publish new pointer then wait grace period before freeing old — reads scale linearly, ideal read-mostly (routing tables, dentry cache).
• Grace period detection: preemption/counters per CPU (classic RCU) or SRCU sleepable variant for arbitrary reader sections.
• Compare-and-contrast answer template: RW lock (readers contend on counter) vs RCU (zero reader sync, writer pays deferred free) vs snapshot structures (persistent copies).
• Userspace analogues: ArcSwap (Rust), COW maps swapped under AtomicReference (Java), immutability-by-default functional designs.
• When NOT RCU: write-heavy, long reader sections, memory-bound reclamation — costs surface elsewhere.

os-deadlocks.title: Deadlocks & Livelock
os-deadlocks.intro: The four conditions, prevention strategies, detection tooling, and live incident stories.
groups: Coffman Conditions — Memorize Cold

• Deadlock requires ALL FOUR simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one → impossible.
• Circular wait break = total lock ORDERING (number locks, always acquire ascending) — the industry-default discipline; lint it (clang thread-safety annotations, LockChecker).
• Hold-and-wait break = acquire-all-upfront (wasteful) or release-before-new-acquisition; mutual exclusion unavoidable for real resources.
• Preemption break: steal-with-rollback (tx abort semantics) — databases do this via deadlock victim selection.
• Distinguish from starvation (indefinite denial, progress possible elsewhere) and livelock (threads act, make no progress — retry storms).
Prevention Patterns in Practice

• Lock hierarchy documentation + assertion helpers (debug builds verify order) — catches violations at dev time.
• Try-lock escalation: acquire secondary with try_lock; on failure release primary and backoff-retry — avoids blocking cycles, adds latency variance.
• Single-lock-per-object discipline; composite operations move INTO the owning object (monitor pattern) instead of callers juggling multiple locks.
• Timeouts everywhere (pthread_mutex_timedlock, PG lock_timeout) convert hangs into errors — pair with retry budgets and alerting.
• Immutable/shared-nothing architectures sidestep entirely: message passing (actor model), ownership (Rust compile-time proof!).
Detection & Recovery

• Runtime detection: wait-for graph cycle detection (databases: SQL Server/PG deadlock detectors kill cheapest victim, return error to loser — application retries).
• Tooling: jstack/jcmd Thread.print (look for BLOCKED holding chains), gdb thread apply all bt, pstack; TSan/Valgrind-HG race+deadlock analysis in CI.
• eBPF/off-CPU profiling reveals lock waits invisible to CPU flamegraphs — brendangregg off-CPU analysis method.
• Recovery playbook: capture dumps FIRST (evidence dies on restart), identify cycle, decide restart vs targeted unlock, add regression test reproducing interleaving.
• Distributed deadlocks: edge-chasing/probe algorithms exist but practically avoided via timeout+saga compensation — say that.
Dining Philosophers & Canonical Problems

• Philosophers: resource hierarchy (everyone picks lower-numbered chopstick first) breaks circularity; asymmetric solution (odd/even order) also works; arbitrator/central waiter serializes acquisition.
• Readers-Writers: policy flavors (reader-pref → writer starvation; writer-pref → reader starvation; fair/phase-fair balances) — choosing policy IS the interview answer.
• Producer-Consumer: bounded buffer with two condition variables (notFull/notEmpty) — know the missed-signal bug when notify happens outside lock.
• Cigarette smokers / barber variants test push toward formal thinking; barbershop = semaphore counting capacity + FIFO queue fairness discussion.
• Sleeping barber lesson generalized: bounded queues apply backpressure BEFORE unbounded waiting piles up.
Database-Level Locking Traps

• Classic MySQL/PG deadlock: txn A updates row 1 then row 2; txn B row 2 then row 1 — fix: consistent row order in all code paths (ORDER BY id for batch updates).
• Gap/next-key locks (InnoDB RR) widen deadlock surface on range scans; RC isolation reduces them (tradeoff phantom protection).
• FK-triggered cascade locks surprise people: parent delete locks children rows implicitly — index the referencing column or eat surprises.
• Schema migrations: ALTER TABLE ACCESS EXCLUSIVE queues behind long transactions AND blocks newcomers behind it — use lock_timeout + retries, pg_repack for big rebuilds, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
• Monitoring: pg_stat_activity wait_event=Lock, innodb_print_all_deadlocks, deadlock counters trended as SLO.
Livelock & Starvation Stories

• Livelock signature: 100% CPU, zero progress — two threads politely retrying against each other; fix: randomized exponential backoff breaks symmetry (Ethernet CSMA/CD lesson).
• Priority starvation: RT threads starve CFS, big readers starve writers, fat tenants starve neighbors — mitigations: aging, quotas (cgroups), admission control.
• Thundering herd as collective livelock: broadcast wakeup stampedes — wake-one semantics, staggered timers (jitter!), epoll EPOLLONESHOT patterns.
• Retry storms after dependency brownout amplify outage — retry budgets (cap % of requests), circuit breakers, hedged requests with caps.
• Case study format for interviews: symptom → diagnosis tool → root cause → fix → guardrail added. Practice narrating one from each category.

os-memory-mgmt.title: Memory Management
os-memory-mgmt.intro: Allocators, fragmentation, NUMA, huge pages — the layer between malloc() and silicon.
groups: Virtual Memory Recap With Numbers

• 48-bit VA → PML4/PDPT/PD/PT walk (4 memory refs worst case on TLB miss); CR3 swap per context historically flushed TLB — PCID tags avoid most of that today.
• Latency ladder: L1 ~1ns, L2 ~4ns, L3 ~15-40ns, DRAM ~100ns, NVMe read ~50-100µs — every caching design decision reduces to these gaps.
• Page fault taxonomy: minor (~0.1-1µs, map existing), major (~50-200µs NVMe, ms on HDD), protection fault (COW break, mprotect enforcement).
• Overcommit defaults let malloc succeed beyond RAM+swap; strict mode 2 fails allocation early — DBs commonly prefer failing loud.
• OOM killer scores badness (RSS − oom_score_adj); protect critical daemons with adj=-1000, watch PSI memory pressure instead of guessing.
malloc/ptmalloc Internals

• Chunks carry size headers inline; bins organize free chunks: fastbins (small, LIFO, uncoalesced), unsorted/small/large bins (doubly-linked, best-fit-ish).
• Arenas: per-thread heaps (main arena via brk, others mmap'd) reduce lock contention — M_ARENA_MAX tunable; too many arenas = fragmentation sprawl.
• Trim behavior: free() returns memory to OS only at heap top (brk shrink) or whole non-main arenas — mid-heap frees leave RSS resident (the 'why doesn't RSS drop' classic).
• mmap threshold (>128KB default, dynamic) routes large allocations straight to anonymous mappings — freed wholesale, avoids fragmentation, pays TLB shootdown on munmap.
• Debugging: MALLOC_CHECK_, valgrind massif (heap profiles), jemalloc prof_active heap sampling, ASAN for UB.
tcmalloc / jemalloc Design

• Size classes: round requests to ~80-200 classes; per-thread caches serve most allocations lock-free; central page heaps manage spans.
• jemalloc: extents/arena chunks, decay-based purging (dirty pages linger configurable time before madvise) — smooths RSS sawtooth; tcmalloc: span-based with background release rates.
• Why services adopt: contention reduction at high thread counts + fragmentation containment via size-class discipline; Go's runtime is tcmalloc-inspired.
• Swap-in cost: allocator choice affects TLB misses and cache locality measurably (few % to tens % on allocation-heavy microbenchmarks).
• Operational knob familiarity: MALLOC_CONF (jemalloc), TCMALLOC_* env vars — production memory tuning lore worth mentioning.
Fragmentation Anatomy

• External: free memory scattered in too-small holes — classic with interleaved size distributions and long uptimes; metric: RSS flat-high while live bytes low.
• Internal: rounding waste inside size classes (avg half-class per object) — acceptable tradeoff, quantify with class histograms.
• Mitigations: size-class allocators, slab reuse pools for fixed-type objects, periodic arena release, restart-on-threshold (last resort, embarrassingly common).
• C++ specific: custom pools for hot small objects (protobuf arenas!); string interning for dedup; reserve+shrink vector patterns.
• Diagnose: heap profiles over time, /proc/PID/smaps rollup (anon vs heap segments), mallinfo/malloc_stats snapshots.
NUMA & Cache Topology Awareness

• Per-socket memory controllers: local ~90ns vs remote ~130-140ns class; numactl -H shows distances (10 local / 21 remote typical).
• Policies: default first-touch, bind, preferred, interleave; bandwidth-bound workloads sometimes WANT interleave despite latency hit.
• First-touch trap: initialization thread touches everything → all pages on its socket; fix: init threads per-node or migrate_on_fault later.
• Tools: numastat -p PID, perf stat -e node-loads/node-stores, lscpu topology flags; pin IRQs/app threads consistently (IRQBALANCE off for tuned servers).
• False sharing redux: perf c2c finds bouncing lines; pad, align, per-core copies then aggregate.
Huge Pages & TLB Economics

• 2MB/1GB pages slash TLB miss pressure for GB-scale working sets (one entry covers 512× more memory); DB buffer pools love explicit hugetlbfs.
• THP (transparent): convenient but background compaction/khugepaged stalls cause latency cliffs — Postgres/Oracle/Redis guidance often defrag-disable + madvise-only.
• Quantify: workload walking 10GB randomly: 4KB pages need ~2.6M TLB entries churned; 2MB pages ~5K — miss-rate math makes the argument vividly.
• PCID interaction: tagged TLB keeps per-process entries across switches — combined with huge pages, translation overhead nearly vanishes for hot loops.
• Tradeoffs: internal fragmentation for sparse regions, migration difficulty (compaction), memory pinning reduces reclaim flexibility.
resources: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory

os-virtual-memory.title: Paging & Virtual Memory
os-virtual-memory.intro: Replacement algorithms, COW mechanics, swapping policy — the exam favorites asked with production twists.
groups: Address Translation Walkthrough

• Split: [16 unused | PML4 | PDPT | PD | PT | offset12]; each table = one 4KB page of 512 entries. LA57 extends to 128TiB VA.
• PTE bits: present, rw, user/supervisor, accessed, dirty, NX, global. Hardware page-walker caches intermediate levels independently (paging-structure caches).
• ASLR randomizes segment bases per exec — exploit mitigation costing nothing steady-state.
• Segmentation vestigial in long mode except fs/gs bases (TLS, per-CPU areas).
• Exercise: given VA hex, extract indices and walk tables — occasionally literally asked in low-level rounds.
Page Replacement Theory

• OPT/Belady baseline (evict farthest-future use) — unrealizable benchmark; FIFO suffers Belady's anomaly (more frames CAN mean more faults); LRU stack-algorithm immune.
• Practical approximations: clock/second-chance (reference-bit sweep), aging counters (periodic shift), Linux active/inactive lists + refault detection reconstructs working-set distance.
• Working-set model: keep pages touched in Δ window; thrash when Σ working sets > frames — detect via majflt/s explosion + PSI stalls.
• Global vs local replacement: global lets hot process borrow (fairness risk); local isolates (fragmentation of effort) — Linux global with cgroup-aware reclaim middle ground.
• NUMA-aware reclaim and per-node LRUs (modern kernels) — mention as current sophistication.
Demand Paging & Copy-on-Write

• Lazy everything: text faulted on execute, .bss zero-page-shared until write, heap grown on touch — RSS grows as used, not as mapped.
• fork(): COW page tables; write fault clones ONE 4KB page at a time. Redis BGSAVE rides this for instant snapshots.
• Cost model: fork time ∝ page-table size (~20MB PTEs for 10GB at 4KB pages) + TLB shootdowns; THP makes granularity 2MB — faster fork normally, brutal COW storm during child writes (Redis disables THP, official docs).
• vfork/posix_spawn skip duplication entirely for exec-immediately cases; spawn combines CLONE_VM|CLONE_VFORK safely.
• MAP_PRIVATE anonymous = COW-from-zero-page; MAP_SHARED file-backed = coordinated with page cache — know which mapping type your library chose.
Swapping Policy & Modern Alternatives

• Swappiness (default 60) biases anon vs page-cache reclaim; swappiness=0 still swaps under real pressure (common misconception!) — cgroup memory.swap.max controls harder.
• zram/zswap: compress swap pages in-RAM (3-4x density) — ChromeOS/embedded standard, gaining server traction for burst absorption.
• SSD swap viable with NVMe latencies; still 1000x RAM — treat as safety net not extension; database servers traditionally disable entirely (stall unpredictability).
• MADV_DONTNEED drops (refault pays full price) vs MADV_FREE lazy (reads see stale until pressure) — subtle semantics interviewers probe.
• Monitor: vmstat si/so, PSI memory some/full, majflt rates per-process (pidstat -r).
OOM, Pressure Signals & Tuning

• oom_badness = RSS+swap−oom_score_adj×total; victims logged with dump — postmortem reading skill expected at senior level.
• PSI (pressure stall information): /proc/pressure/{memory,io,cpu} quantifies stalled-time fractions — the modern alerting basis replacing free-mem heuristics.
• earlyoom/systemd-oomd userspace killers act before kernel OOM (latency-driven victim choice) — increasingly standard on desktops/servers.
• cgroup v2 memory.high (throttle near limit) vs memory.max (hard, OOM beyond) — layered protection for multi-tenant hosts.
• Tuning drill narrative: app got OOM-killed at 3am → check PSI history, find leak vs spike, set memory.high guard, fix leak, add RSS trend alert.
MMU Exotics Worth Knowing

• Userfaultfd: userspace page-fault handlers — live migration, dedup tricks, fuzzers pause-on-access; powerful niche API.
• Memory tagging (ARM MTE): tags catch UAF/overflow at hardware granularity — Android adopting; future of memory safety discussions.
• SEV/TDX confidential computing: encrypted guest memory, MMU plays with protected ranges — cloud security angle.
• KSM (kernel samepage merging): dedup scans — VM consolidation trick, side-channel caveat.
• Huge-page shattering on NUMA balance/migration — why THP+NUMA rebalancing interacts badly; defrag settings trade CPU for availability of huge pages.

os-file-systems-io.title: Filesystems & I/O Models
os-file-systems-io.intro: From open() to flash: VFS layers, journaling crash semantics, page cache, and epoll→io_uring progression.
groups: VFS Objects & Path Resolution

• Four pillars: superblock, inode (metadata/extents), dentry (name↔inode cache), file (open instance+offset). Everything-is-an-fd falls out naturally.
• Path walk grabs dentry cache per component; RCU-walk lockless fast path falls back to ref-walk under contention; symlink resolution recursive with limits.
• Hard link = extra dirent to same inode (nlink++); symlink separate inode storing a path; directory hard-links forbidden (cycle prevention).
• fd semantics: dup'd fds SHARE file offset; independent opens don't; O_APPEND makes offset+write atomic per call.
• inotify/fanotify for change watching; statx richer metadata; io_uring also does statx/open/close async now.
Journaling & Crash Consistency

• Journal records intent → commit block → checkpoint later; ext4 ordered mode journals metadata only, data written before associated metadata commit (no stale-data-after-crash exposure).
• Drive write-cache reordering defeated by barriers/FUA — disabling barriers 'for speed' corrupts after power loss (never prod).
• Reason-through scenarios: append+crash (partial record detectable via checksums), rename-during-write (old-or-new never torn IF fsync discipline followed), replay idempotence.
• CoW filesystems (ZFS/btrfs): never overwrite in place; new blocks + atomic root-pointer swing → snapshots/free, checksums end-to-end; cost: write amplification + fragmentation tendencies.
• Application-level equivalents: WAL+fsync+checksum (SQLite/LevelDB pattern) — same theory above the kernel; great bridge in interviews.
ext4 vs XFS vs btrfs/ZFS

• ext4: extents, delayed allocation, HTree dirs; boring-in-a-good-way default; online grow only.
• XFS: allocation groups scale parallel metadata; king of big-files/huge-dirs; reflink CoW clones; RHEL default — safe DB host choice.
• btrfs: checksums, subvolumes, transparent zstd compression, send/receive; RAID56 historically shaky. ZFS: ARC, raidz, snapshots first-class, dedup RAM-trap flag.
• F2FS flash-aligned log structure; overlayfs layers container images; NFS/9p network edges.
• Selection narrative: correctness features vs raw parallel performance vs operational maturity — replication usually lives ABOVE the fs anyway.
Page Cache & Writeback Control

• read() populates cache; write() dirties pages; writeback threads flush per dirty_expire or dirty_ratio thresholds — bursty writeback = latency cliffs (tune per-cgroup writeback v2).
• fsync durability contract: forces data+journal; fdatasync skips mtime metadata (cheaper, enough when size unchanged); syncfs whole-filesystem.
• Atomic publish recipe: write temp → fsync(temp) → rename → fsync(parent dir) — the full incantation, ask candidates to recite it.
• O_DIRECT bypasses cache (DB self-managed buffers); alignment requirements; posix_fadvise shapes readahead/DONTNEED drops (scraper hygiene).
• mmap vs read(): mmap wins random access + zero-copy sharing, loses fine-grained fsync control and pays fault costs — LevelDB optionally mmaps, Postgres prefers own pool.
Blocking → epoll → io_uring

• Thread-per-connection hits C10K walls (stack memory, scheduler thrash); select/poll O(n) rescans; epoll registers interest once, epoll_wait returns ready set O(ready).
• Edge-triggered (EPOLLET) fires once per transition — drain till EAGAIN required; level-triggered simpler, slight extra syscalls.
• Reactor pattern (nginx/Redis/envoy): demux events → dispatch handlers. io_uring shifts to Proactor: submit queued ops, completions arrive in rings; batching 64 ops amortizes syscall overhead dramatically (Axboe demos >1.7M IOPS/core).
• io_uring scope: read/write/fsync/accept/connect/sendfile/statx — one submission language for all storage/network ops; registered buffers/files cut per-op setup further.
• Zero-copy family: sendfile/splice kernel-side plumbing; MSG_ZEROCOPY tx registration; NIC-level RDMA for the exotic tier.
Storage Device Layer Numbers

• HDD: seek ~5-10ms dominates; sequential ~200MB/s; queue sorting (NCQ) helps adjacent-ish requests.
• SATA SSD: rand read ~90µs; FTL mapping + GC causes write amplification; TRIM (discard=async mount) reclaims; steady-state ≠ spec-sheet SLC-cached burst.
• NVMe: 64k queues×64k depth, ~10-20µs, multi-GB/s; poll-mode queues shave interrupt latency; enterprise PLP capacitors make flush honest (consumer drives may lie!).
· Durability testing culture: fio --verify with power-cut rigs for firmware honesty; quota semantics vary by vendor — trust but measure.
• Capacity planning: DWPD endurance ratings, over-provisioning for sustained writes, temperature throttling curves on dense chassis.

os-kernel-syscalls.title: Syscalls & Kernel Interfaces
os-kernel-syscalls.intro: How user code enters the kernel, sandboxing surfaces, tracing tools, and the interfaces every senior engineer should name.
groups: Syscall Path Anatomy

• libc wrapper sets number in rax, args in rdi/rsi/..., executes syscall instruction → kernel entry (MSR-configured trampoline) swaps to kernel stack, validates pointers (copy_from_user), dispatches table[ax].
• Cost: ~60-300ns depending on Spectre mitigations/retpolines — motivates vDSO (gettimeofday), batching (io_uring), and avoiding chatty APIs.
• Return convention: negative errno in kernel; libc translates to -1 + errno. EINTR semantics on slow paths: SA_RESTART auto-retry vs explicit temp-failure loops.
• seccomp-BPF filters syscall numbers/args — Docker default profile blocks obscure vectors; audit via seccomp notify (supervising process emulates).
Tracing & Observing the Boundary

• strace -c -p PID aggregate; -e trace=%file,%network filters; overhead caveats (ptrace stops). perf trace lighter-weight; bpftrace one-liners attach prod-safe.
• Examples worth memorizing: bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:syscalls:sys_enter_openat { printf("%s %s\n", comm, str(args->filename)); }'
• /proc introspection: PID/status, sched, io, fd/ symlinks (leak hunting), maps, smaps_rollup.
• eBPF ecosystem: opens doors to latency histograms per syscall without code changes (libbpf tools: syscount, biolatency).
• Audit trails: auditd rules for execve/file access compliance; structured logs beat grep archaeology.
Capabilities & Sandboxing

• Root monolith broken into capabilities (CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE for :80, CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE...) — drop everything else post-start (prctl PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS + cap dropping).
• Landlock LSM: unprivileged filesystem sandboxing policy in-process (modern, composable); AppArmor/SELinux system-policy alternatives.
• seccomp user-notification turns syscalls into RPC decisions — FEX/Box64 emulation and advanced sandboxes built on it.
• Container escape classics to reference: kernel vulns (namespaces aren't security boundaries alone), /proc/sysrw misconfig, capability leaks, privileged mounts — defense in depth argument.
• macOS/Windows contrast: seatbelt/sandbox, AppContainer tokens — portability awareness flex.
Time, Timers & Clocks

• CLOCK_REALTIME (wall, NTP-disciplined, jumps), CLOCK_MONOTONIC (since boot, never jumps — USE FOR TIMEOUTS), CLOCK_BOOTTIME includes suspend.
• timerfd/posix timers integrate deadlines into epoll loops; coarse vs precise latency/cost tradeoffs; slack for batching.
• NTP/chrony/PTP: strata, slew vs step; leap smears; VM clock drift stories — distributed-systems adjacency (TrueTime contrast!).
• High-res timing pitfalls: TSC invariant cores, rdtsc serialization issues, clock_gettime vDSO path is what you want.
• Timer wheel internals (kernel hrtimer/timerfd scalability) — mention casually if probed on timer-heavy servers.
Key Interface Catalog

• Process: fork/clone/execve/wait4/setrlimit/prctl. Mem: mmap/mprotect/madvise/mlock/userfaultfd.
• IO: read/write/pread64/sendfile/splice/epoll*/io_uring_setup/enter. Net: socket/setsockopt(TCP_NODELAY!)/bind/listen/accept4.
• IPC/sync: futex/eventfd/shm_open/memfd_create (anonymous tmpfs — sealed memfds for plugin safety!).
• Namespaces: unshare/setns/clone flags. Caps/security: capset/seccomp/landlock_create_ruleset.
• Knowing WHICH syscall solves a class of problem (memfd for anonymous executables, io_uring for batched IO, userfaultfd for lazy loading) is the senior signal — quiz yourself listing one use per interface.

os-interview-classics.title: OS Interview Classics
os-interview-classics.intro: The rapid-fire bank: canonical questions with model answers anchored in concrete numbers.
groups: Numbers You Must Recite

• Syscall ~60-300ns (mitigation-dependent); vDSO call ~2ns. Context switch 1-5µs direct, up to ~100µs cache-refill indirect.
• Thread create ~10µs; fork 10GB RSS ~ms-scale (page tables); minor fault ~0.1-1µs; major fault NVMe ~50-200µs, HDD ~ms.
• Loopback TCP RTT ~30-60µs; unix socket ping-pong ~2-5µs; shared-memory ping-pong sub-µs.
• DRAM ~100ns vs NVMe ~100µs vs HDD seek ~7ms — the 1000x steps justify every cache tier.
• Use numbers to JUSTIFY designs: batching, pooling, pinning, huge pages — quantified reasoning is the senior tell.
Concept Rapid-Fire With One-Line Answers

• Process vs thread: address-space isolation vs shared-everything; switch costs differ accordingly.
• Mutex vs spinlock: park-vs-burn; choose by hold-time vs switch-cost ratio.
• Virtual memory purpose: isolation, overcommit, COW, paging flexibility — not just 'more memory than RAM'.
• Buffer vs cache: write-behind staging vs read-ahead reuse; page cache unifies both for files.
• Soft vs hard IRQ: top/bottom halves; deferring work keeps latency bounded (tasklets/workqueues/threaded IRQs).
• Daemon vs service vs job: detached session, supervised unit, scheduled batch — systemd vocabulary modernizes the answer.
Scenario Drills (Tell Your Story)

• 'Server latency spikes every night 2am': cron/logrotate/backup IO storms — correlate with iostat util%, PSI, journal commit bursts; mitigate ionice/cgroup caps, schedule staggering.
• 'RSS climbs forever but heap profiler flat': fragmentation or native leaks outside traced allocator — jemalloc profiling, smaps anon growth, arena stats.
• 'App slower in container than VM': cgroup CPU throttling periods (cpu.max quota burstiness), memory.high reclaim churn, noisy siblings — check throttle stats before blaming overlayfs.
• 'fork slow in big service': huge RSS page-table copy + THP interactions; consider posix_spawn, snapshot via COW-friendly design, or pre-forked worker pools.
• 'Disk full though du disagrees': deleted-but-open files (lsof +L1), sparse file illusions, overlay upper bounds, reserved blocks (tune2fs -m).
Design-Flavored OS Questions

• 'Build a rate limiter at process level': token bucket with monotonic clock, CAS refill, sharded counters to dodge contention.
• 'Implement a job queue on disk': WAL append + fsync batching + in-mem index + compaction — mini-Kafka reasoning.
• 'Zero-downtime config reload': SIGHUP handler swapping immutable config snapshot (RCU-flavored), draining connections, dual-listener overlap window.
• 'Watch 10k files efficiently': inotify watches + recursive dir management, fallback fanotify mount-level; discuss watch limits (max_user_watches).
• 'Ship a binary that runs anywhere': static musl vs glibc NSS plugins tradeoff, seccomp profiles, OCI packaging — modern pragmatics.
Behavioral-Technical Hybrids

• 'Worst production incident you've debugged?' STAR format with OS forensics: timeline, tools (sar archives! dmesg timestamps!), hypothesis elimination, fix + guardrail.
• 'How do you decide kernel upgrades?' LTS cadence, CVE watch, canary fleet, rollback plan (kexec/dual-boot partitions), livepatch for emergency CVEs.
• 'Convince me to adopt io_uring': measure-first pitch — profile syscall overhead share, prototype hot path, feature-gate fallback, team ramp plan; mention maturity/compat caveats honestly.
• 'What would you remove from Linux?' Thought question — they're probing mental models: e.g., legacy SysV IPC vs modern primitives, THP defaults debate — argue both sides.
• Close with questions showing depth: their kernel versions, eBPF posture, io_uring adoption, PSI-based alerting — interview the interviewer.
